title: Seattle, Washington
seoTitle: Charter Bus in Seattle, Washington: Group Travel Guide
excerpt: A charter bus in Seattle handles the hills, the traffic and the parking. The stops worth a group's time, vehicle sizing, and where coaches can actually load.

heroImage.alt: The Space Needle above the Seattle skyline with Elliott Bay and the Olympic Mountains behind

extraImage.alt: Fish stalls and crowds under the neon sign at Pike Place Market

body.text: Seattle is built on a series of steep hills between a lake and a sound, with a downtown core that has almost no room to spare. For a group that means two things: the walking is harder than the map suggests, and parking a vehicle is expensive where it is possible at all. A charter bus in Seattle solves both, provided the day is planned around where a coach can legally stop.
The stops worth a group's time

items: Pike Place Market: the fish throwers, the original Starbucks, and the produce stalls. Busiest before noon and genuinely crowded — give a group ninety minutes and a firm meeting point.
Seattle Center: the Space Needle, Chihuly Garden and Glass, and the Museum of Pop Culture all within a few minutes' walk of each other. The most efficient stop in the city for a group.
The waterfront and Seattle Aquarium, at the bottom of the hill from Pike Place.
Pioneer Square: the oldest part of the city, with the Underground Tour beneath it — a genuinely good ninety minutes and a favorite with school groups.
The Museum of Flight, south of downtown: a Concorde, the first Air Force One, and a Blackbird. Ample coach parking and a strong half day.

body.text: Where a coach can load

Pike Place Market has no coach parking and the streets around it are narrow, steep and permanently congested. The workable arrangement is a drop-off on First Avenue and a collection at an agreed point away from the market entrance. Seattle Center and the Museum of Flight are both far easier and have proper provision.

Downtown hotels are practiced at loading groups. What does not work is a vehicle waiting on a hill in Belltown or Capitol Hill, and a driver unfamiliar with the city will discover the grades the hard way.
The hills change the itinerary

Several downtown blocks are genuinely steep, and the walk from the waterfront up to Pike Place is a serious climb rather than a stroll. For a group with any mixed mobility, plan the walking legs downhill and let the coach do the uphill work.

It is the single most useful piece of Seattle planning there is, and it costs nothing — being dropped at the top and collected at the bottom completely changes how the day feels for anyone who would otherwise arrive at every stop out of breath.
Which charter bus suits a Seattle itinerary

items: Forty to fifty-six: a full-size [charter bus](/fleet/motor-coaches) is right for a conference group or a school trip, and works well for the outlying stops and day trips.
Twenty to thirty-two: a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) is considerably easier inside the city, reaching hotel loading zones and neighborhood streets a coach cannot.
Ten to fourteen: a [sprinter van](/fleet/sprinter-vans) suits an executive group working between downtown and the Eastside.
Twenty-eight to sixty: a [school bus](/fleet/school-buses) is economical for districts within about ninety minutes.

body.text: Conference and offsite movement between downtown, South Lake Union and Bellevue is a large part of what we run here, handled by our [corporate travel](/services/corporate-travel) team, with Sea-Tac arrivals covered by our [airport transfer service](/services/airport-transfers).
Day trips from Seattle

Seattle is an excellent base. [Mount Rainier](/blogs/mount-rainier-washington) is about two and a half hours south, [Olympic National Park](/blogs/olympic-national-park-washington) two hours plus a ferry or the long way round, and Leavenworth's Bavarian-themed streets around two and a half hours east over Stevens Pass.

The Washington State Ferries also make Bainbridge Island an easy half day — walk-on passengers need no reservation, and the crossing itself is thirty-five minutes of the best view of the city there is.
Traffic is the schedule, not the distance

Seattle has some of the worst congestion in the country for a city its size, largely because the geography leaves nowhere for the roads to go. Interstate 5 through downtown is a bottleneck in both directions for most of the day, and a fifteen-minute journey at ten in the morning is comfortably forty-five at half past four.

Plan the outlying stop early. The Museum of Flight, Boeing's Everett factory tour and any Eastside destination should sit at the start of the day rather than the end, and a group heading back to a downtown hotel in the evening peak should expect the return leg to take roughly double.

The ferry terminals are the other pinch point. Colman Dock sits right on the downtown waterfront and the line for a sailing can back up into city streets, so a group with a booked crossing needs a departure time set well before it feels necessary.
When to go

July through September is the reliably dry season and the only time Mount Rainier is consistently visible from the city. May, June and October are pleasant and much quieter. From November to April expect gray and persistent drizzle rather than heavy rain, which suits a museum-weighted itinerary and disappoints anyone hoping for the postcard skyline.
